In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections . And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power .
In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”
“It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”
He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”
During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.
I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in?
Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so.
I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. And the thing that struck me most was the level of security.
Obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these big fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it.
Then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby.
It was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that.
Before I read your book, I thought of data centers as something that’s important, but a little bit boring. How did you decide they were interesting and rich enough to sustain an entire book?
I felt the same. I was aware that data centers had been out there, but it was not something that I was paying particularly close attention to. But then there were a number of stories that of tipped me off to the fact that there might be more here, and that it was worth looking deeper into what was going on — the first being hearing about the water pressures created by data centers in Chile around the capital of Santiago , where companies like Google and Microsoft were building data centers, and communities were concerned about their access to water and started organizing around that.
And then hearing about how much electricity data centers were consuming in Ireland, to the point that now they consume more than 20% of the country’s electricity , and that was obviously pushing up power prices. It was putting pressures on the grid, such that the grid operator actually put a moratorium in place for grid connections for data centers around the Dublin area, back in 2022. This was even before the generative AI moment that caused a surge in construction of data centers.
And then the other one was in The Dalles, Oregon, where Google had actually built its first company-owned data centers about 20 years back. In that case, its water deal was coming up for renewal. It wanted to build more data centers there, so it needed more water. And when the residents started asking, “How much water is Google actually using?” a journalist at The Oregonian went to the city and essentially asked, “Hey, how much water is Google using? Our readers would like to know this,” he was hit with a lawsuit instead of being given that information. Because Google did not want it to be public. And then, of course, when it did come out about a year later, Google revealed that it was using 29% of the city’s water, which seemed quite significant.
That was around when ChatGPT was being released and generative AI was starting to take off. It felt like, okay, there are these pockets of places where a lot of data centers have already been constructed, where they are putting pressures on the communities that are causing people to respond, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities. It was a good time to really start to dig in and pay attention.
You don’t just talk about the data centers’ environmental impact, but also, they [become] your way in to talk about this broader tech moment. They represent to you — particularly the hyperscale data centers — represent to you how these tech companies are doing business now.
Absolutely. The hyperscale data centers and just the scale of the construction — whether it’s the the size of the actual facilities themselves or the number that these companies are trying to build out, just feels fundamentally unsustainable.
They’re just demanding too much from the communities where they’re being located, whether that’s because of electricity or because of water use or what have you, or just the fact that they’re building out so many, that when you think about the cumulative impact and you look at the demand for water, but particularly for energy from fossil fuels, that means that it’s just completely out of line with a livable planet and an amount of computation that feels like it makes any degree of sense for us to have constructed.
I think it really goes back to the hubris of the tech industry and of these major tech companies and the tech billionaires that run them, and the fact that they have these particular visions of the future that are based on fantasies , but also on expanding their own power and influence over the world, and they don’t seem to mind that everyone else then has to pay the cost that comes with their ambitions and what they are seeking to do.
And I feel like it’s become particularly egregious wit…

Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis
A mathematician at Anthropic has said that the San Francisco -based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics – and experts say the claim checks out.
Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks.
On Saturday afternoon, two organizations announced that they had independently verified Alpöge’s claim after reviewing the programming language he used to share the solution.
The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems.
“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”
Alpöge linked to computer code – written in a language called Lean – that he maintained could verify the findings.
Mathematicians subsequently began working to see if Alpöge’s proof could be confirmed. On Saturday afternoon, the Lean Focused Research Organization – which seeks to advance the use of the programming language – and the Mathlib Initiative, a program that works with Lean for math equations, announced that they had verified Alpöge’s solution.
“We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the groups announced.
Alpöge’s note was published just one day after Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. He acknowledged that, writing: “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier.”
The Riemann hypothesis is a nearly 170-year-old math problem named after Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician who proposed it in 1859.
The hypothesis deals with prime numbers – whole numbers greater than 1 that can only be divided by themselves and 1. Riemann questioned how often prime numbers appear and how they are distributed along the number line. And he developed a formula for estimating how many prime numbers existbelow a specific number.
The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium prize math problems selected in 2000 by the Clay Mathematics Institute. The institute has offered $1m for each problem solved.
Mathematicians have been attempting to solve this problem for years. The New York Times reported that on Friday, an independent mathematician in Italy released an incomplete proof of the Riemann hypothesis that he said he had been working on for almost 12 years. That mathematician, Alessandro Masullo, said he did not use AI because he did not fully trust the system.
Other mathematicians have expressed discomfort with relying on AI to solve math problems.
In September, Anthropic competitor OpenAI claimed that a non-public version of its AI tools helped solve part of another Millennium prize problem. But it was solved in a way that struck mathematicians and observers in a way many found strange: a near-trillion-dollar private company spent $15m to employ 10,000 AI systems to solve the problem.
Alpöge was working on that separate problem for Anthropic when OpenAI made its announcement.
This story was edited on 22 November 2026 to account for updated information: the Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative statement claiming to verify the solution was added, and a quote from a prior story from a mathematician was removed, as updates to the news evolved

The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music . Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto -themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site.
Creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus , doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere.
Within hours of the discovery, Nicalis shared on X that Repentance Plus had been updated and the generated music files had been removed . While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” users on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “ uninspired and bland ” in a TikTok from 2024.

The debut LP from Sheherazaad blends traditional Indian instruments with Western electronic flourishes and feminist narratives.
Sheherazaad started making ripples in the music world a few years ago with her EP Qasr , which was produced by Grammy Award winner Arooj Aftab . Now she’s back with Khudgarzi , her reverb-drenched folk-noir debut LP that’s primarily sung in Urdu.
The instrumentation on Khudgarzi draws on traditional South Asian music, including Carnatic and Hindustani styles, but also dabbles in Arabic folk traditions, as well as modern Western electronic music. Trip-hop flourishes and Spaghetti Western guitar brush up against tanbur and ghatam. Sheherazaad’s stunning voice sits atop dripping percussion and seasick drones singing about the plight of “The Selfish Woman.”
For Sheherazaad, the character of the selfish woman isn’t the villain, it’s a charge leveled at women who didn’t conform to societal norms, “ eccentric women whose desire for agency was often met with an awful end .” Even if you can’t understand most of the lyrics, the atmosphere tells the story clearly enough. From the barely simmering anger of “Registaan” to the bleak repetition of “Qatil” and the fantastical yearning of “Zeher,” Khudgarzi is clearly the work of a woman exploring what it means to be a woman, the lasting legacy of colonialism, and the perpetual threats of a patriarchal society.
Khudgarzi is alternately a funeral dirge and a celebration of femininity. Sheherazaad owes a lot of the album’s ability to navigate these various themes and moods to her impressive production work, top-notch mixing by J. Valleau, and the cast of over 30 “genre-chaotic” virtuosic musicians including Ria Modak, Sarathy Korwar, Jay Chakravorty, Shunya, and Qasim Naqvi. The instrumentation never distracts, though. It’s not showy, and all emulsifies around Sheherazaad’s vocals in a shawl that feels equal parts comforting and oppressive.
Khudgarzi is available now on Bandcamp and most major streaming platforms, including YouTube Music , Spotify , Apple Music , Deezer , and Qobuz .

Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and, now more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility !
Waymo pulling its robotaxis off freeways (again) and Zoox robotaxis launching on the Uber app illustrate the push and pull between progress and setbacks in the autonomous vehicle industry.
There are signs of growth. For instance, Tesla has now surpassed Waymo in Texas in the number of robotaxis registered with the state (Tesla has 1,507 and Waymo has 1,345). But does that translate to market dominance?
A better metric, if we’re trying to gauge who is leading, would be commercial driverless miles. And if we’re measuring cost-efficiency, another useful metric would be driverless miles per vehicle. By those measures, Waymo is still ahead, based on data available to me. But with Waymo’s recent freeways setback and Tesla’s push to expand its robotaxi fleet with Cybercabs, that lead could shrink.
Not that there needs to be a winner, by the way. Transportation is deeply fragmented, and there is room for multiple players in the U.S., not to mention the rest of the world.
A recent discussion with my Autonocast co-host Ed Niedermeyer, whose book, “Elon Take the Wheel,” comes out December 1, got me thinking about how Las Vegas could soon become a real world A/B test of sorts for human-driven vs. autonomous ride-hailing services.
Uber, as mentioned above, just added Zoox to its ride-hailing app in Las Vegas. For now, riders don’t have much of a choice. Uber customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi, and they can always decline a robot ride. But they can’t directly select a robotaxi. Instead, Uber riders will be matched with one if it’s available.
Uber said that will soon change. The company plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.
Las Vegas will also become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app, he said. (Hyundai’s self-driving subsidiary Motional is also an Uber partner.)
That would give Uber riders a meaningful choice: a human driver or a robotaxi, and potentially even which autonomous service to use. And it could offer a revealing look at what customers actually prefer when given that choice. Price could tip the balance, too.
It makes me wonder whether Las Vegas will become the next battleground for organized labor as robotaxis begin competing directly with human drivers.
You might have seen the Wall Street Journal scoop that General Motors is working with an executive search firm to identify possible candidates to replace CEO Mary Barra . Rumors of her imminent departure have swirled for months, but this time there appears to be real work happening behind the scenes.
I reached out to a few little birds to learn more and here’s what they’re telling me. And, for the record, GM declined to comment.
GM has hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles, according to one source, who noted it’s possible that the board has other executive search firms working on this as well. The board is taking a two-track approach to its search, which is occurring simultaneously.
The first is focused on traditional yet transformative automotive CEOs. One name that has come up from the executive search firm is José Muñoz, who is president and CEO of Hyundai. The board is also interested in someone less traditional. The firm has apparently floated names like Doug Field, who recently became CEO of Mind Robotics, and Larry Culp of GE, according to a source with direct information.
There are internal GM folks who are also in the mix, including Sterling Anderson, co-founder of self-driving trucks company Aurora who became chief product officer at GM in May 2025, and Paul Jacobson, the company’s executive vice president and chief financial officer.
Got a tip for us? Email Kirsten Korosec at [email protected] .
Elysian Aircraft , the Dutch aerospace company developing aviation electrification technologies, raised €12 million in private and public funding from FideFlux, SecFund, and ROM InWest, as well as from individual investors and family offices.
Mahindra Last Mile Mobility , an electric three-wheeler business under Mahindra & Mahindra, is looking at an IPO in about 18 months, per Bloomberg .
Numa , a startup developing an AI operating system for dealerships, raised a $45 million Series C round led by New York-based Blue Cloud Ventures. Threshold Ventures, Costanoa, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures, and Tokio Marine Future Fund also participated.
Stark Future , a European electric motorcycle company, raised at least €150 million in equity, Reuters reported. The raise was led by Highland Europe, alongside Morgan Stanley Investment Management’s 1GT and Axon Partners Group.
Vincue , an automotive tech company that sells software to dealerships, raised $93 million in a round led by Wavecrest Growth Partners, with continued backing from FM Capital.
Also , the electric micromobility startup that spun out of Rivian last year, has paused deliveries of its new e-bike over problems with its software and batteries, The Verge reported .
Edmunds released new data that found the average new vehicle is selling for a record $50,087.
Redwood Materials is using computer vision and machine learning to identify and sort batteries by chemistry before they’re fed into the company’s rotary calciner — a massive cylindrical industrial furnace used to process 40,000 metric tons of raw feedstock a year.
Tesla said it will spend about $3.3 billion to expand its Berlin gigafactory to produce Cybercabs — yet another signal of the company’s global autonomy ambitions.
Over the weekend, Tesla invited “select customers” to preorder the company’s autonomous, golden Cybercab “for personal use.” The Cybercab is priced at $29,990, but there is a lot more to ownership. The company will charge owners $299 a month to use the vehicles, delivery will only occur in a handful of cities, and operations will be limited to specific locations.
Uber opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities. Uber already has a service for teenagers. If this program proves successful, it would open Uber up to another market of customers: busy families.
Meanwhile, Uber said it’s notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal information was stolen in an October data breach.
Zipline continues to scale its autonomous drone delivery business, this time in its partnership with Uber. The companies had previously announced a partnership for drones to deliver for Uber Eats, but it officially launched this week in a Houston suburb. The aim is a big one: Uber and Zipline say they aim to make 1 million deliveries a day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.
I had a chance to catch up with (and interview) Ro Gupta , the head of Woven Capital — Toyota’s growth fund.
I’ve known Gupta for years; we first met when I worked at Fortune and he had a startup called Carmera. A lot has happened since those AV 1.0 days, and Gupta caught us up on this next era of AV innovation and where Toyota is interested in investing. It’s not enough to simply state “AI.” There’s more to it than that. Take a listen .

Transparency International says Queensland’s David Crisafulli was ‘by far the most frequently accessed’ state leader, with 13 meetings
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Bosses at 10 datacentre companies secured almost 120 meetings with premiers and ministers in five states over a three-year period, with experts declaring this is “just the tip of the iceberg”.
Analysis by Transparency International Australia argues these meetings, when combined with political donations, demonstrate “unfettered access” to decision-makers that creates an “uneven playing field”.
The report found donations from major datacentre companies and their contracted lobbying firms nearly tripled over the past three years from $685,000 to $1.8m, coinciding with increased investment across Australia.
The analysis found the Queensland leader, David Crisafulli , was “by far the most frequently accessed state premier”, with public diaries showing he has met datacentre executives 13 times in the past three years.
This included three meetings in as many weeks in August and September with Australia’s largest datacentre operator, NextDC – roughly one month before the company’s expansion in Melbourne was halted after its power provider delayed construction of new power poles due to community backlash .
“Those meetings took place shortly before the Queensland premier announced a dedicated framework to fast-track datacentre approvals by taking them out of the hands of local councils,” the Transparency International report said.
Crisafulli has embraced datacentre investment and flew to the United States in September to secure a $31.9bn deal with the AI giant Anthropic for what could become Australia’s largest datacentre . His office was contacted for comment.
During this three-year period, 119 meetings with ministers or premiers were held in New South Wales , Victoria, Tasmania, Queensland and the ACT. These are the only jurisdictions to publicly release ministerial diaries. The meetings were mostly held in 2026.
“These numbers are just the tip of the iceberg,” said Clancy Moore, the chief executive of Transparency International Australia.
“What we don’t know is how many meetings companies like NextDC, OpenAI and Anthropic and their third-party lobbyists are having with the prime minister and ministers in our federal parliament.
“Australia’s lobbying laws also don’t cover in-house lobbyists or government relations staff so there’s very little oversight of their activities too.”
The report also found Australian company Firmus Technologies secured 10 meetings with Tasmanian ministers and the premier this year alone. During this period, the company’s expansion in the state has faced sustained backlash from local communities who feel they were not properly consulted .
The three companies that secured the most meetings with ministers were Amazon Web Services, Macquarie Technology Group and NextDC.
Last month, Guardian Australia reported on political donations from Amazon and Macquarie to both major parties, closely aligning with the announcement of multimillion-dollar government contracts or planning developments. Both companies say these donations were not aimed at influencing policy and that their timing was coincidental.
A shareholder at NextDC’s annual general meeting on Friday said the company had “a lot of lobbying going on in Canberra” but called on the company to better lobby the public on the benefits of datacentres.
The company’s chair, Stephen Flynn, said he was “not sure we are great at lobbying as an industry or as a company” but the world had now changed.
“We thought we were just going along and [being] invisible, in the way if you think about all telecommunications systems … [it] is kind of invisible. We just take it for granted. But we can’t do that. We can’t do that as we go forward.”
The report has also cited examples of four senior public servants at federal government departments quitting to assume leadership positions at OpenAI, AirTrunk and CDC. Three of these appointments were made this year.
In September, the president of the Australian Professional Government Relations Association, Sally Mackenzie, said the scale of engagement between industry and ministers was a sign of the system working as intended.
“What we’re seeing with AI and datacentres is that dynamic playing out at real pace, because the stakes for industry, government and Australians more broadly are so high,” Mackenzie said.
“Lobbying is an important part of the democratic process. It ensures that all stakeholders have the ability to communicate with government.”

Auracast broadcasts are an integral part of the storytelling in this off-Broadway show about love, connections, and hearing loss.
Up a few concrete steps and through the front door of a 200-year-old row house in New York City, I follow a crowd of people into the 178-seat SoHo Playhouse. As we filter to our seats, ushers hand each person a black drawstring bag with a pair of wired headphones connected to a small Auracast receiver . Then, soon after the play begins, we’re instructed to put them on.
The headphones are an integral storytelling tool of Love Me — a one-man show from the minds of stand-up comedian and former Saturday Night Live writer Drew Michael and director Prashanth Venkataramanujam. It’s a show about love and the bid for connection, told in five chapters about different relationships in Michael’s life, bound by the threads of his hearing loss and self-discovery.
Love Me ’s experimental sound design is possible thanks to Auracast, a technology based on Bluetooth that can broadcast a high-quality audio stream to any number of nearby devices. As the show follows Michael from childhood through adulthood, sound designer Daniel Kluger uses the headphones in combination with the theater speakers to create experiences that wouldn’t be possible with a traditional setup. Tinnitus ringing and hearing test tones play in the music between sections as subtle clues as the show builds to Michael’s epiphany about his hearing loss. Kluger also explores the world through varying levels of sonic clarity. Sound playing through the theater’s speakers is sometimes intentionally muffled, which is then further dulled by the headphones, giving the audience a sense of what Michael is hearing in those moments.
But one sound that stays clear and pristine is Michael’s inner monologue, heard in the headphones throughout the show. The inner monologue consists of both prerecorded tracks and the live feed from Michael’s microphone on stage as he talks back and forth with himself. “Any time you’re in my head — anything in the headphones is coming through clearly,” Michael tells me after the show. “[We’re] trying to also highlight that the appeal of the inner world is such that it’s the highest fidelity space for this person. It’s more comfortable.”
The different sound sources and treatments of the sound can lead to intentionally confusing scenes for the audience. During one, where Michael is doing a stand-up set at a comedy club, three sounds compete for attention: The theater speakers play the crowd’s reactions (including a heckler whose voice is sometimes muffled and sometimes clear); his prerecorded inner monologue reacting to the crowd plays in the headphones; and on stage, Michael is performing the set, with his mic muffled so our focus is on his inner monologue. It’s one of the definitive moments where the audience feels the constant concentration necessary to parse what’s happening when sounds aren’t clear and become overwhelming.
But the biggest impact comes during a climactic scene the sound design has been building toward, a realization that also incorporates the visuals of a series of Michael’s audiograms over the years. “I had this massive breakthrough about the whole history of what I’ve been doing — the cognitive labor, the invisible to myself labor that was affecting every single minute of my life,” Michael says. “That was a huge moment.”
That’s when the audience is instructed to remove the headphones we’ve been wearing for nearly the entire show. As Michael comes to the recognition of his relationship with his hearing loss and the clarity of mind that gives him, what we’ve become used to for the entire show’s experience — the headphones — are now gone, as is that literal weight from our heads. It’s an emotional moment, one that I’ve thought about multiple times since seeing the show.
It also leads into the final act, where Michael begins to understand his own Deaf identity. “The deafness is not the culprit, it’s the denial of it.” he tells me. “My hearing currently has never been worse, but I’ve never been more self-affirmed or self-actualized or felt happier in myself. It’s a misconception, I think, about deafness as a tragedy, deafness as a deficit, deafness as a burden, deafness as something that plagues a person.”
The ability of Auracast to broadcast an audio stream that any number of headphones can connect to is what made Love Me a possibility. Any Auracast headphones can connect to the audience broadcast — I brought along the Nothing Pro 1 to test the ability and connected to the audience broadcast channel in seconds — but I used the provided Auri receiver and Austrian Audio headset for the performance. The show’s sound was designed with those in mind, and I didn’t want the differing isolation of the Nothing headphones to affect the intent of the experience.
Love Me is presented in partnership with Deaf West Theatre , which supports Deaf-centered storytelling in theatrical productions. In addition to the audience Auracast feed, there’s one for users of hearing aids and cochlear implants that’s designed for compliance with those devices, and iPads with captions are also available. During the performance, Michael connects to his own broadcast channel with Auracast-enabled Phonak Eon Sphere hearing aids. “We talked about using in-ear monitors, but if I use an in-ear monitor, then I don’t have amplification from my environment, so then I lose contact with the audience,” Michael says. “These function as two things: They’re hearing aids and also in-ear monitors.”
Love Me relies on the Auracast technology to tell its story, but it isn’t a story about hearing technology. The technology is there to tell the story of connection and discovery of identity. “I think right now … there are two things that are at odds — the hearing aid and audiological tech side of deafness and then the cultural identity side of deafness,” Michael says. Technological improvements, like cochlear implants and hearing aids, are cited as one of the reasons schools for the deaf have been on the decline, which leads to kids being mainstreamed (put into regular public schools) and losing out on Deaf history and culture. “I’m not against the tech,” Michael says, “I just think tech and Deaf identity should be a marriage rather than a divide.”
And that collaboration is why Love Me works as well as it does. The Auracast technology is there both for accessibility — in the same way it’s already used in other performances, lectures, or announcement systems — and to uplift the show’s story of love, acceptance, and acknowledgement of one’s own Deaf identity. It’s an inventive use of the technology that carries with it a powerful message.

For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED.
The organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry. Unlike an LED TV, which creates images by shining a backlight through a panel of pixels, OLEDs leverage millions of self-lighting pixels, which provides significantly better pixel control, and can generate a much more nuanced image with deeply vibrant colors and a more intense light and shadows.
They are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years. However, this year I couldn’t wait any longer. I finally sprang for an upgrade and, since I was already upgrading on image quality, I decided to upgrade the size, too: I bought a 65-inch LG evo C4, which is the company’s mid-range unit released in 2024.
At first, the experience was amazing. The television rendered colors and shadows wonderfully and, seeing as one of the goals with this purchase was to indulge my physical media habit, I began running through my collection of 4K Blu-ray discs with the madcap energy of a true fanatic.
However, things took a bit of an unexpected turn when, midway through “McCabe and Mrs. Miller,” I was suddenly overcome by a wave of nausea. I’m not particularly sensitive to motion sickness, but this sensation — which made it feel vaguely like I was going to hurl — persisted for several hours after it initially began. It was then replaced by a small tension headache.
I discovered that this is actually a somewhat common experience for new OLED adopters. Indeed, Reddit is rife with posts from new television owners who claim they feel like their big new toy is breaking their brain.
“I got the tv yesterday and still feel sick today,” one Redditor , who said they had recently purchased an LG C2, wrote. “Feel light headed and nauseous a day later. Thinking about taking it back. Is this normal? I’m scared to turn the thing on lol.”
Others blamed the sheer size of the screen. One guy, who bought an 85-inch TLC, claimed it had led his wife to the conclusion that “it’s too big and say that she feels sick watching. Is that a thing that a screen can be too big?”
There doesn’t seem to be a consensus on why this happens. Many Redditors blame certain motion-smoothing settings. However, my TV did not come with those settings enabled. Others blamed viewers for sitting too close to the screen — yet I was sitting a solid nine feet away, which is well within the recommended range for a 65-inch screen.
Finally, others have argued that the screen brightness could be agitating users’ eyes. I dialed down the brightness on mine to around 50 percent, although I had doubts as to whether this actually had anything to do with the feelings I was having.
In considering my nausea, one theory that sprang to mind was that it might just be my eyes’ inexperience with viewing such a big screen. The TV was so large that it often felt like my eye had to trace different parts of the screen to take in the whole picture and, if the scene involved significant motion (most movie scenes do, after all), it conjured the sensation of trying to stare too intently at something out the window of a moving car.
After a few days, however, my eyes finally adjusted. The nausea was gone. All that remained was an immense and beautiful home viewing experience that made every previous viewing experience pale by comparison.
Initial physiological reactions aside, the size of the 65-inch screen (and whether your living space actually has room for it) is still something that needs to be considered carefully by potential buyers. I recently moved into a place with a slightly bigger living room, which has given me the flexibility to install a bigger device. At my old apartment, however, this size of TV would have definitely felt like it was devouring the space.
Another slight frustration is that the C4 does not come with any detailed installation instructions. The screen (which is so wide it’s difficult to move without another person there to help you) comes detached from its base, and the user is just sort of expected to figure out how to effectively move and put together the two pieces. A quick YouTube video is all that is necessary to understand this process, but you have to be careful when moving and assembling the pieces so as not to scratch or damage the screen.
Once the whole thing is set up and assembled, the OLED is a truly beautiful thing to behold. The customization that’s possible, including advanced brightness and color control — and things like “Filmmaker Mode” (which claims to adjust each movie’s color and frame rate settings to those intended by the director) — make the user experience really powerful.
To sum up: The evo C4 is a really spectacular piece of equipment that has a lot to offer the avid home entertainment viewer — although there may be a bit of a learning curve before it makes your cinema dreams come true.

The European Union has formally rejected the latest COP31 draft deal, saying it cannot accept an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels.
Darragh O'Brien, the climate and energy minister for Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency, said the EU and its member states "object" to the draft because it "does not meet the moment."
"We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya Pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change," O'Brien said.
The announcement could see the chaotic and late-running climate talks collapse.
A new COP31 draft agreement had been published early on Sunday as nations continued to struggle to reach an accord.
The new draft kept a much-sought goal to electrify the global economy but again failed to mention fossil fuels, deepening divisions at the UN conference - which is being held in Antalya, Turkey.
The latest text needed consensus approval from almost 200 nations at a closing session on Sunday.
An EU official had told the AFP news agency that the draft was a "backwards" step and warned that there was a "very real possibility" of the talks ending without a deal.
"I am more pessimistic today than I was yesterday," they said.
"The situation is difficult, and the outcome is uncertain. The oil-producing countries are putting up a fierce fight," a German official added.
Planet-heating fossil fuels have become a flashpoint at the talks, which come amid soaring energy prices and simmering global tensions stemming from the Iran war.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week had called for a sped-up phasing out of fossil fuels. But a second version released on Thursday removed all mentions of the energy sources, forcing negotiators back to the bargaining table.

The latest offering acknowledged a previous global deal to transition away from fossil fuels but stopped short of naming them explicitly.

EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey .
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”
As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.
The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.
But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels.
The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.
“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”
Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop.
In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.
His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.
“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.
But Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, who called it “the worst Cop ever”, said: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create ... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.
“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”
Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations. Pakistan told the conference that just because a few items in the pact were objectionable to some, the rest should not be sacrificed: “Climate action is not a menu from which we can select only what suits us.”
Ghana also had criticisms of the process but did not reject the final text: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”
Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.
The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.
Asked about the consensus-based system that broke down at the talks, Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN framework convention on climate change, said: “It certainly fell short today,” while emphasising that a significant number of agenda items were passed, with “real progress and concrete results”.
But for many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis.
While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño , the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.
“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “I am deeply disappointed that Cop31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

A powerful explosion aboard a Russian vessel docked at Libya’s eastern port of Benghazi has raised concerns that the Russia-Ukraine war could be extending into North Africa, after local authorities suggested the ship may have been targeted in a drone attack.
Officials from Libya’s eastern administration said the explosion occurred on Sunday while the Russian ship was stationed at the port for refuelling and resupply before returning to Russia.
No casualties were reported, although the incident prompted an emergency response and heightened security concerns around the port.
In an official statement, the eastern authorities indicated that drones were suspected of striking the vessel. No group or government immediately claimed responsibility.
The administration also emphasised that Libya was not involved in the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, seeking to distance the country from any suggestion that its territory was being used as a battleground in the ongoing war.
Early accounts of the explosion suggested that a fire had erupted at an ammunition storage facility within a naval installation in Benghazi. However, Libya’s eastern authorities subsequently clarified that the blast originated aboard a Russian ship docked at the port.
Local television reports described emergency crews being dispatched to the affected area to contain the fire and prevent it from spreading to nearby facilities.
Al-Masar television, citing civil defence personnel, reported that firefighters had been deployed to a military facility following the explosion. Libya Alhadath television also reported that residents were advised to avoid the surrounding area while emergency operations were underway. The fire was later brought under control.
Although Libyan authorities did not identify the vessel or disclose details of its cargo, naval analysts have provisionally identified it as the Russian missile corvette Merkury, which is believed to have sustained extensive damage in the explosion.
Libya’s eastern-based government announced plans to conduct a joint investigation with Russian officials to establish the circumstances surrounding the explosion.
The Benghazi incident comes against the backdrop of increasingly extensive Ukrainian operations targeting Russian military infrastructure, energy facilities and maritime assets beyond the conventional battlefield.
According to the supplied reports, a Russian cargo vessel was struck by a drone in the eastern Baltic Sea on Saturday , near Finnish waters. Finland’s military said Ukraine was likely responsible for the attack, although Kyiv has not claimed responsibility.
Although no evidence has been publicly presented linking Ukraine to the Benghazi explosion, the timing has drawn attention to the growing geographical reach of attacks associated with the war.
Russia has previously accused Ukraine of targeting vessels involved in transporting Russian energy exports, including ships operating far from the Black Sea.
The latest developments have raised questions about the vulnerability of commercial shipping routes, port facilities and maritime logistics networks in regions traditionally considered outside the immediate conflict zone.
The suspected strike has also exposed the security challenges facing Libya, where competing political authorities continue to exercise control over different parts of the country.
The internationally recognised Government of National Unity, based in Tripoli, expressed concern about the possibility of civilian maritime infrastructure being drawn into foreign military operations.
In a statement, the Tripoli administration warned against using Libyan ports and other civilian facilities for activities connected to international conflicts.
It stressed that Libya should not become a staging ground for foreign military confrontations or logistical operations that could threaten national security and sovereignty.
The statement reflects broader concerns that Libya’s strategic Mediterranean location, combined with its prolonged political fragmentation, could expose the country to escalating geopolitical tensions.
The Benghazi explosion follows other reported incidents involving Russian vessels in and around the Mediterranean.
In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier was severely damaged off the Libyan coast following an attack. Russian President Vladimir Putin blamed Ukraine for the incident, although responsibility remained a matter of dispute.
The vessel was reportedly associated with Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, a network of ships used to transport Russian energy exports while navigating Western sanctions and restrictions.
Ukraine has previously acknowledged operations against vessels linked to Russian maritime trade, including an attack in the Mediterranean in December of the previous year.
Such incidents have intensified concerns over the potential consequences of maritime attacks, particularly near civilian ports and international shipping corridors.
Apart from the immediate threat to vessels and crews, explosions involving ships can pose risks to port workers, coastal communities, commercial operations and the marine environment.
Russia has maintained longstanding military and political relationships with influential actors in eastern Libya, including forces associated with military commander Khalifa Haftar.
Libya’s geographical position makes it strategically important for access to the Mediterranean, North Africa and the wider Sahel region.
The country has remained politically divided since the 2011 uprising that overthrew longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi. The internationally recognised administration in Tripoli, headed by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, continues to face a rival eastern political and military establishment supported by Haftar.
This fragmentation has complicated efforts to establish unified national security institutions and limit foreign military involvement.
For now, significant questions remain unanswered, including whether the explosion was caused by a deliberate drone strike, who may have carried it out and whether the vessel was transporting military equipment.
The planned Libyan-Russian investigation may provide further information about the incident, although any conclusions will require examination of the available physical and technical evidence.
If a deliberate attack is confirmed, it would raise fresh concerns about the possibility of Russia’s war with Ukraine affecting ports and maritime facilities in North Africa.

UN climate talks collapsed on Sunday as the European Union ​and others rejected a final draft deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkey and Australia , saying it was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.
The failed talks reflect world governments' struggle this year to muster ambitious action to address the worsening consequences of climate change , as wars, economic pressures and other crises compete for their attention.
After more than two weeks of negotiations ​that spilled two days into ‌overtime – making it the longest COP on record – Turkey's conference president Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that he could see ⁠there was no agreement and confirmed he would not advance any new text.
"There is nothing to do, we did all that we could," he said. "There will be no new text from now on."
He later left the stage in the midst of speeches ‌being delivered by country representatives.
Australia's COP31 President of Negotiations, Chris Bowen, called the outcome "very disappointing" and said disagreements over fuels and climate finance were the ⁠dealbreakers.
The last time UN climate talks failed to get a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009.
Ireland's environment minister Darragh O'Brien said the European Union could not support the proposed deal in part because it made no mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say drive global warming.
"It is unconscionable that ​we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels," he said.
"Time is ticking and we are not there yet," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said in a statement.
Belgium's Climate Minister Jean-Luc Crucke said the failure of the deal was a difficult outcome, but appropriate.
"It's ​not the end of multilateralism, but there has to be courage to say no," he said.
Saudi ‌Arabia and other big oil producer countries had lobbied hard to keep their mention out of the text, according to observers at the summit.
Panama also said it could not support the text because it failed to address the scale and urgency of the climate crisis.
This year's COP is the first since the UN's environmental body in October confirmed the rise in global temperature was set to exceed ‌1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), a threshold countries agreed at Paris climate talks over a decade ago to try not to exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify.
Reacting to the news, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply disappointed" that the talks in ended without consensus.
"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," Guterres said in a statement.
"Those who profit from the destruction of our planet must never dictate the terms of the fight to save it. Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis," he added.
While a blow to efforts to ratchet up international action, the failure to agree a political declaration in Antalya does not erase the obligations agreed by previous UN conferences or remove the technical and legal frameworks governing multilateral action against climate change.
Read more COP31 climate talks go into overtime as nations wrangle over fossil fuels omission
The failed deal had acknowledged the planet's projected temperature overshoot and called for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse it.
While scientists say removing carbon from the atmosphere – when paired with steep emissions cuts – is vital to ​avoiding the worst impacts of climate change, critics of the proposed deal said they worried the carbon removal language would be used as a licence to keep pumping oil.
A representative for the Saudi delegation, which supported the deal's mention of carbon removal, told the summit ​at the closing plenary that he was surprised at the resistance to technology, which he said offered a concrete solution.
Developing countries had also criticised the deal for not providing sufficient new climate finance to help them adapt to a warming planet. The deal had called for a tripling of such finance, but did not specify from what baseline.
The failed deal had also included a goal put forward by Turkey to expand electricity's share of total final world energy consumption to 35% by 2035, from around 23% now.
Proponents of that pledge said it could cut greenhouse gas emissions ⁠by speeding the transition away from fuel-powered cars, furnaces, and other equipment. But critics said it could force more costs onto poor nations without providing a clear path away from fossil fuels.
The COP process is the main vehicle ⁠through which countries coordinate their efforts ​to curb global warming. Its annual meeting provides an opportunity for nations to signal they are willing to work together to find solutions and help finance the problems rising temperatures cause.

Last year, I nearly quit mathematics. On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics?
In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. I was stunned.
I earned my PhD in 1993 and built a life around research, teaching, and mentoring. I’d love to prove that Ramanujan’s tau function never vanishes, or that half of the partition numbers are even. My 25-year-old self would have been crushed by what we are witnessing today. Nothing I write can reassure someone just starting a career. I can explain why I stayed.
My father, a number theorist, died in January. As a boy, I learned from him about Ramanujan, whose notebooks have occupied mathematicians for generations. Ramanujan believed a Hindu goddess gave him mathematical formulas in his dreams. When I considered working on AI, I feared my father would see it as abandoning mathematics. Instead, he told me AI reminded him of Ramanujan: discoveries from an unexpected source might leave us much to understand. I do not take that comparison literally. Ramanujan was a human with an extraordinary imagination and life. My father’s response brought me to tears. It gave me permission to keep being a mathematician in a way I had not anticipated.
Today, I am on leave from the University of Virginia and work as Founding Mathematician at Axiom Math. We use AI to formalize, verify and extend mathematical proofs in Lean, a language in which a small checking program verifies each step. This work can expose gaps and make proofs inspectable and reusable. Human judgment remains essential: we must check that the formal statement says what we intended.
We released the first complete Lean formalization of the classification of finite simple groups, one of mathematics’ largest proofs. Announced in 1983, the classification required decades of work by many mathematicians; a major gap was filled in 2004. Our AI helped produce 43.1 million lines of Lean code. In the process, we found a problem in a published route to a key theorem and supplied an alternative argument. Lean’s kernel checks the resulting formal proof. The mathematics belongs to the generations who developed it. Our formalizations of the classification and other bodies of math are already helping us build and check further mathematics.
After 24 days of work, I watched the final milestones land on my laptop. I cried. I thought about the people who had made the classification possible, and about the father I could no longer tell. But I am 58. I’ve advised 35 PhD students, 17 postdocs, and hundreds of undergraduates. I’ve had opportunities young mathematicians cannot assume. I cannot ask a graduate student to regard uncertainty as an adventure because I have found rewarding work within it.
At a Berkeley colloquium two days after OpenAI announced its Navier–Stokes solution, a scheduled lecture became a town hall lasting almost two and a half hours. Students asked about credit, transparency, hiring, and how mathematicians whose work came first were treated. Some asked me what I would do to help them. Campus security was locking the building as we left.
The declaration A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics, signed by Terry Tao and other Fields Medalists, warns about rushed announcements, inadequate attribution and the loss of mathematical understanding. I share those concerns. At a National Academies meeting, I put my position this way: hope is not a plan, and nostalgia is not mentoring.
Universities, journals, employers and funding agencies must decide what they support and reward. Students and younger colleagues should have a voice while those decisions are still open, as should mathematicians who choose to work without AI. In the discussions where I have a voice, I will argue for that participation.
Students need room to struggle with mathematics and learn to question the tools they use. In my advising, I will ask what a young mathematician understood, originated, or made possible. Access to a powerful system is no substitute for those contributions. For work I help publish, readers should know what has been proved, what remains assumed, and who contributed the ideas.
I want my students, and their students, to develop ideas that are genuinely their own. I want them to have colleagues who listen and the material support to pursue a mathematical life. My work at Axiom is one part of how I am trying to contribute. It does not replace my obligations as a teacher and mentor. I may be wrong about how this will unfold. I am still learning what it means to be a mathematician.
Ken Ono is a number theorist and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, currently on leave as founding mathematician at Axiom Math. A former vice-president of the American Mathematical Society, he is known for his work on Ramanujan and integer partitions.
These views do not necessarily reflect those of Axiom Math, the University of Virginia, the National Academies, or any other institution with which I am affiliated.

A joint select committee report on Monday should signal where Labor is headed on issues including datacentres and copyright – and whether they’ll go it alone
Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast
T he final four days of parliament for 2026 begin on Monday, and the government has a clutch of key reforms, budget hangovers and savings measures it wants to pass. But how many, if any, will get over the line by Friday is anyone’s guess.
But over the top of the usual last-week-of-school feeling of parliament at this time of year, between the Christmas parties, frenzied negotiations and the prospect of Senate all-nighters, hangs the protean multi-headed beast of AI. An eagerly anticipated parliamentary report will drop this week, bringing us one step closer to Labor’s long-awaited legislation on datacentres, energy use and copyright – just as the green shoots of a bipartisan consensus on AI threatens to split.
Several key policies remain in Senate limbo: the domestic gas reserve, changes to trusts and capital gains tax, the digital duty of care bill, and changes to private health insurance. Labor sources are confident some will get up this week, and the re-entry of Anthony Albanese into the domestic political fray after a week in Manila and Shenzhen is expected to intensify deal-making.
Labor sources expect they are closer to a deal with the Coalition on gas, while the Greens are the more likely partner on the rest of the slate. But the Greens and Coalition are in no mood to give Labor any quick wins. One Greens source says they would be surprised if much passed at all this week.
The Liberal deputy leader, Jane Hume, told me on the Australian Politics podcast on Friday that she was happy to see “movement” on gas , as Labor promised a carveout for Western Australia – a key Coalition demand – but said was “more they could do”, particularly around long-term supply. Talk of the government entertaining a gas phaseout, as pushed by the Greens, was seen by both the Coalition and Greens as just a tactic to pressure Angus Taylor and frighten business groups; at this stage, don’t expect to see a Greens-Labor deal on fossil fuels.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
On digital duty of care, the Treasury bills and private health, though, the minor party is closer.
Both Labor and the Greens have publicly maintained that negotiations remain up in the air, each are telling the other that the ball is in their court. Greens sources have for some time said they don’t feel any pressure to cave on CGT and trusts, and are relatively content with the status quo on private health, so might hold out for the amendments they want.
Digital duty of care, however, is likely to find some agreement. The parliamentary report handed down on Friday, chaired by Labor, only recommended the government make one of the key amendments requested by the Greens, to allow a private right of legal action for citizens to take big tech to court. The Greens also want bigger fines, an ombudsman for big tech and further restrictions on gambling. Labor is keen to get this done and say they are open to amendments.
It may not get the biggest headlines this week but potentially the most interesting development may come as soon as Monday. That’s when the joint select committee on artificial intelligence is expected to release a report that could signal where Labor will go on the thorniest issues, such as datacentres and how Australian creatives should be paid for the AI theft of their work.
The report will also signal whether AI policy will remain a relatively bipartisan endeavour, as some Liberals have recently proposed, or whether the major party alliance will fracture.
The creative industries were flabbergasted last week when reports about Labor considering a carveout for music in a permit system for AI companies landed the morning after the Aria awards – where Elton John, Tim Minchin and other well-loved musicians lined up behind the Not AI’s To Take campaign .
Many creatives say they strongly doubt that the government was seriously considering such a proposal. But what’s not in doubt is senior Labor figures have begun more forcefully claiming there are shortfalls in copyright law – despite major rightsholder groups rubbishing the need for change . From Richard Marles to Tim Ayres and Michelle Rowland, a rejection of the “status quo” has bubbled up, potentially pointing to a direction of travel.
Liberals Jonathon Duniam and Aaron Violi just a fortnight ago said AI was “too important to become an unnecessarily partisan political contest”. But the shadow attorney general, Michaelia Cash, labelled the potential music carveout a “ham-fisted tactic”, saying property should not be “stolen”. Influential Liberal MP Garth Hamilton suggested AI was “just good old-fashioned theft”, proposing companies be subject to a levy. The former Nationals leader David Littleproud said on social media: “I reckon Anthropic can afford to pay everyone for copyright now. Don’t let big AI bully us!”
The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong , will on Tuesday make a major speech to parliament to raise AI as an issue of foreign policy and national security. According to advance notes, she will say the development of AI must not “reward speed over prudence” and urge a “shared, global endeavour” that Australia wants to help shape.
“That means building trust between countries, cooperating when things go wrong and making sure the world’s response matches the power of the technology,” Wong will say.
But, at least for this week, all eyes will be on how the federal parliament’s response matches up.
Josh Butler is a political reporter and the Guardian’s Canberra bureau chief of staff

A Russian navy corvette docked at the Benghazi naval base ​in eastern Libya was hit on Sunday by a suspected Ukrainian sea drone, according to local officials, in what appeared to be the latest attack linked to the Russia-Ukraine war in the North African nation. Hours later, a cargo ship was also hit by a sea drone in a second attack off Benghazi on Sunday evening.
A suspected Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship Sunday at a naval base in Libya , officials said, the latest attack in the North African nation linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.
The strike at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials told the Associated Press.
They said that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.
Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Muammar Gaddafi , who was later killed, in 2011. A UN-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.
Read more Russia turns to Libyan ports after Assad's ouster in Syria
The eastern Libya-based government said in a statement that the strike on Sunday caused an explosion and fire at the base, which was later extinguished.
The vessel had docked at the base for refueling and supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said, without providing details on the vessel or its cargo.
A joint investigation was launched with Russia to “uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it,” the statement said.
No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack. There was no immediate comment from either Russia or Ukraine .
On Sunday evening, local media said that another sea drone hit a commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi in a separate attack.
Local officials said a "merchant vessel was targeted this evening by explosive-laden sea drones off the coast of Benghazi", but did not specify whether the ship had been Russian as well.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for either strike, but they come as Ukrainian forces have stepped up long-range barrages against Russia far from the front lines.
Reports said the second ship was sailing under a Maltese flag.
The eastern Libyan administration said all crew members had been rescued and were receiving treatment for minor injuries.
Libya Alhadath television later reported that naval and air force units intercepted more than 12 "explosive-laden sea drones" off Benghazi.
No further details were given. The Almasar satellite television channel said that naval and air forces destroyed at least 12 other sea drones off the Mediterranean city.
The western Libya government expressed concerns about “dragging Libyan ports and civilian facilities into external conflicts,” in an apparent reference to the war in Ukraine.
“The government reaffirms its categorical rejection of turning Libya into an arena for international conflicts or a theater for external powers to settle scores,” it said in a statement.
In March, Ukrainian forces operating in western Libya under a covert deal struck a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in a suspected sea drone attack near Maltese waters, Libyan officials said at the time.
The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, operated mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also at other military facilities in the capital, Tripoli, and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press.

What have I learned from my experiment with outsourcing? That I’m easily replaced – and awful
I ’ve just ventured deeper into my phone’s settings than anybody has ever been before. A software update is always discombobulating, but the latest one brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense (that mental image you just got of me waving my fist at the sky: spot on). Even when you manually switch off Apple Intelligence, check the box to make Siri the same dummy she’s always been, and deselect the option to offer replies to texts and emails, it makes no difference. Harrumph.
Days later, bored on the bus, I began answering my husband’s texts with the terrible suggested AI responses, to see if he’d notice. (We’ve been married a long time; this is how I get my kicks now.)
Mortifyingly, notice he did not. Even when I told him, “You’re a classic!” and laughed “Haha I know right” with nary a comma.
There was worse to come. Because that-which-shall-eventually-rule could tell I’d used its proposed sentences, it was encouraged, and proposed more, which I was tutting and scoffing at until it recommended a reply that ended with the nickname I call my husband. Not darling, honey, or whatever – something unique.
A chill descended in my soul as the penny dropped that these weren’t generic phrases everyone gets – they were specific. My phone was impersonating me, showing me who I really was, and – long story short – I was awful. Cheesy, exclamation-mark-addicted, and full of bantz with a definite z.
Humbled in a way it is probably impossible to ever fully recover from, I realised that in conducting this experiment, I had utilised the very artificial intelligence I was battling to remove just hours before. I’d hate-used it, yes, but I’d used it all the same. Further proof, not that it was needed, that resistance is futile. Luckily I surrendered immediately and have always been fully on board with AI, so when the day comes, I’ll be absolutely fine. Haha I know right.

“All elements of the joint SAR [search-and-rescue] team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field,” he added.
Rizky said four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic.
